stem: The determinant \(D = \begin{vmatrix} a & b & a+b \\ b & c & b+c \\ a+b & b+c & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0\) if
_note: Derivation: \(C_3 \to C_3 - C_1 - C_2\) makes the first two entries of \(C_3\) zero and the third \(-(a+2b+c)\), giving \(D = -(a+2b+c)(ac-b^2)\). So \(D=0 \iff b^2=ac\) (a,b,c in G.P.) OR \(a+2b+c=0\). BOOK DEFECT: the symbol \(\alpha\) in option D never appears in the printed stem. The classic source question prints the third column as \(a\alpha+b,\ b\alpha+c,\ 0\), for which option D reads 'alpha is a root of ax^2+2bx+c=0'; this book has printed \(a+b,\ b+c\) (i.e. alpha silently set to 1), so option D is not a well-formed condition as printed. Answer B is the option derivable from the printed determinant.
solution: [Textbook misprint: one alternative speaks of \(\alpha\) being a root of \(ax^2 + 2bx + c = 0\), but \(\alpha\) appears nowhere in the printed stem. The determinant factors as \(-(ac - b^2)(a + 2b + c)\), so it vanishes either when \(ac = b^2\) — that is, when \(a, b, c\) are in G.P., the keyed alternative — or when \(a + 2b + c = 0\); the \(\alpha\) alternative is the garbled remnant of that second branch. As printed, only the G.P. condition is well formed.]

stem: If \(\begin{vmatrix} x^{k} & x^{k+2} & x^{k+3} \\ y^{k} & y^{k+2} & y^{k+3} \\ z^{k} & z^{k+2} & z^{k+3} \end{vmatrix} = (x-y)(y-z)(z-x)\left(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}\right)\) then
_note: Derivation: taking \(x^k, y^k, z^k\) out of the rows gives \((xyz)^k\begin{vmatrix}1 & x^2 & x^3\\ 1 & y^2 & y^3\\ 1 & z^2 & z^3\end{vmatrix} = (xyz)^k (x-y)(y-z)(z-x)(xy+yz+zx)\). The RHS is \((x-y)(y-z)(z-x)\dfrac{xy+yz+zx}{xyz}\), so \((xyz)^k = (xyz)^{-1}\), i.e. \(k=-1\).

Derivation: expanding gives \(D = \sin^3\theta\cos^2\phi + \sin^3\theta\sin^2\phi + \sin\theta\cos^2\theta = \sin\theta(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta) = \sin\theta\). So \(D\) depends on \(\theta\) only and is independent of \(\phi\); it is not a constant.

stem: The value of \(a\) for which system of equation \(a^3x + (a+1)^3y + (a+2)^3z = 0\), \(ax + (a+1)y + (a+2)z = 0\) and \(x + y + z = 0\) has non zero Soln. is
_note: Derivation: a homogeneous system has a non-zero solution iff its coefficient determinant vanishes. With \(p=a,\ q=a+1,\ r=a+2\), \(\begin{vmatrix}p^3 & q^3 & r^3\\ p & q & r\\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} = (p-r)(p+q+r) = (-2)\cdot 3(a+1) = -6(a+1)\), which is zero only for \(a=-1\).

stem: \(\begin{vmatrix} b+c & c+a & a+b \\ q+r & r+p & p+q \\ y+z & z+x & x+y \end{vmatrix} = \)

options.label: A
options.text: \(2\begin{vmatrix} c & b & a \\ r & q & p \\ z & y & x \end{vmatrix}\)

options.label: B
options.text: \(2\begin{vmatrix} b & a & c \\ q & p & r \\ y & x & z \end{vmatrix}\)

options.label: C
options.text: \(2\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ p & q & r \\ x & y & z \end{vmatrix}\)

options.label: D
options.text: \(2\begin{vmatrix} a & c & b \\ p & r & q \\ x & z & y \end{vmatrix}\)

_note: Derivation: the given matrix is \(A\cdot T\) where \(A = \begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\p&q&r\\x&y&z\end{pmatrix}\) and \(T = \begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\1&0&1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}\), \(\det T = 2\); hence the value is \(2\det A\). Options A, B and D are each \(\det A\) with one pair of columns interchanged, so each equals \(-2\det A\).
solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key marks \(2\begin{vmatrix} b & a & c \\ q & p & r \\ y & x & z \end{vmatrix}\). That cannot be the intended answer, because the three rejected alternatives are each \(2\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ p & q & r \\ x & y & z \end{vmatrix}\) with one pair of columns interchanged, so all three are equal to one another; keying any one of them would make the other two equally correct. The alternative keyed here is the one equal to \(2\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ p & q & r \\ x & y & z \end{vmatrix}\).]

\(C_1 \to C_1+C_2+C_3\) makes the first column \(\left(2(a+b+c),\ 2(p+q+r),\ 2(x+y+z)\right)\); taking the factor \(2\) out leaves the first column \((a+b+c,\ p+q+r,\ x+y+z)\).

Now \(C_2 \to C_2-C_1\) turns the second column into \((-b,-q,-y)\) and \(C_3 \to C_3-C_1\) turns the third into \((-c,-r,-z)\); a further \(C_1 \to C_1+C_2+C_3\) turns the first into \((a,p,x)\).

Taking \(-1\) out of each of the last two columns,

\(\begin{vmatrix} b+c & c+a & a+b \\ q+r & r+p & p+q \\ y+z & z+x & x+y \end{vmatrix} = 2(-1)(-1)\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ p & q & r \\ x & y & z \end{vmatrix} = 2\begin{vmatrix} a & b & c \\ p & q & r \\ x & y & z \end{vmatrix}\).

Hence (C).

stem: The system \(3x - y + 4z = 3\), \(x + 2y - 3z = -2\) and \(6x + 5y + \lambda z = -3\) has at least one Solution when
_note: Derivation: the coefficient determinant is \(7\lambda + 35 = 7(\lambda+5)\), which vanishes only at \(\lambda = -5\). At \(\lambda = -5\) the third equation is \(R_1 + 3R_2\) on both sides (\(3+3(-2) = -3\)), so the system is still consistent and has infinitely many solutions. DEFECT (mild): strictly, for every \(\lambda \ne -5\) the determinant is non-zero and the system has a UNIQUE solution, so options B, C and D also give 'at least one solution'. The discriminating case the question intends is \(\lambda = -5\), the value at which the determinant vanishes yet the system remains consistent.
solution: [Textbook misprint and answer-key error: the coefficient determinant is \(7(\lambda + 5)\), so at \(\lambda = 5, 3\) and \(-13\) the system has a unique solution and hence 'at least one solution'. The printed wording is therefore satisfied by all four options and the printed key of C is not distinguishable from B or D. Only \(\lambda = -5\) makes the solution non-unique — there the third equation is \(R_1 + 3R_2\) on both sides, giving infinitely many solutions — so the stem should read 'infinitely many solutions' and the answer is A.]
